Question: How long does protein synthesis take?
Answer: Assuming you mean protein synthesis in a living cell, not in a laboratory, it’s not long at all. It’s so fast it’s hard even to believe it. Plasma cells—the body’s antibody-producing cells (antibodies are proteins)—produce about 2,000 molecules per second (per cell), an average of 0.5 millisecond for each protein molecule. I can’t even say “protein” 2,000 times a second. However, that’s the figure for total cell output, with thousands of ribosomes in each plasma cell working simultaneously to make copies of the same protein. At the level of a single ribosome, it reportedly takes from 20 seconds to several minutes to make one protein molecule. Any cell’s total protein output is at a much greater rate though, because it has thousands of mRNA molecules coding for the same protein being translated at once, and each mRNA being simultaneously translated by typically 10 to 20 ribosomes at once. Here’s one of my textbook illustrations depicting just 8 ribosomes translating a single mRNA. (I show only 8 for artistic simplicity.) Here’s an actual electron micrograph (colorized) showing about 40 ribosomes simultaneously translating the same mRNA. The mRNA is shown in red, the ribosomes in blue-gray, and the proteins spooling off from the ribosomes in green. This is from a cell in the salivary gland of a midge. Imagine 40 ribosomes times many thousand identical mRNA molecules and you can see how one cell can crank out a protein at a phenomenal, imagination-staggering rate.

Question: What nutrition is required when animals are unicellular?
Answer: To start with, there is (by definition) no such thing as a unicellular animal. Being multicellular is one of the characteristics that define animal. Even one of the simplest known animals, Trichoplax, has a few thousand cells of six different types.[1] These animals look like little more than a half-millimeter, pancake-shaped blob of protoplasm, but here’s a diagram of their body wall structure,[2] showing that they’re more organized than a casual observer might expect. Another group of very simple animals is the Mesozoa—tiny wormlike parasites of marine invertebrates—such as Dicyema, a parasite of squid and octopus kidneys. It’s composed of only 20 to 30 cells.[3] These are believed to have evolved from more complex animals by taking on a parasitic mode of life enabling them to discard tissues and cells that no longer served any purpose. But I digress down the pedantic “what is an animal?” trail. You wanted to know about nutrition. All animals, including these, have the same fundamental nutritional requirements as humans and other complex animals: proteins (or the amino acids derived from them), simple sugars (typically derived from larger carbohydrates), fatty acids and other lipids, minerals, vitamins, and water. There are small variations, of course, such as differences in what vitamins a species requires, but all animals are nourished on this basic diet of, so to speak, “six major food groups.” They have diverse modes of acquiring these nutrients, but that’s another matter beyond the scope of your question. Further, if you mean unicellular organisms (more than just animals), then the modes of nutrition must be extended even to photosynthesis. But even then, the basic categories of nutrients remain the same.
